_readme: The application-specific half of the drill. The harness (load-drill.sh, k6 scripts)
knows nothing about Waa; everything app-shaped lives here, so pointing the drill at a
different .NET service is editing this file and nothing else.
'fixtures' are SQL queries run against the restored database before the drill starts.
Each one fills a named list the scenarios draw from at random. This is what stops the
test from hammering a single row: real traffic spreads across slugs, and a benchmark
that reads one row measures the buffer cache, not the database.
'weight' is relative pick frequency within a scenario, not a percentage.

slugs.query: SELECT publicslug FROM events WHERE publicslug IS NOT NULL ORDER BY random() LIMIT 200
slugs.onEmpty: The public-event read is the hot path of this app; with no published events the drill would measure 404s. Restore a dump that has some, or drop the read from 'traffic' below.

traffic.name: public-event-snapshot
traffic.note: The hot path — every invite open hits it. Rate-limited by the 'public' policy (64/min per IP), which is why the harness varies the client IP per VU.

traffic.name: client-config
traffic.note: Fetched on every SPA load, so it rides along with every real visit.

health.note: Exempt from rate limiting by design, so the harness can probe them freely during a drill.

note: ClientIpMiddleware trusts CF-Connecting-IP and X-Forwarded-For from loopback and RFC1918
sources. A drill runs from exactly such a source, so each VU can present its own client IP.
Without this the whole load collapses into one rate-limit partition and the drill measures
the rate limiter (64 req/min) instead of the connection pool — roughly 1 req/s, which would
look like a pass while proving nothing.

_readme: Static headers sent with every request, and the seam for a host that refuses traffic without
a credential. FiscalServer is the case that needed it: every route but /.well-known/ready,
/.well-known/live and the ANAF callback answers a bodiless 401 without a valid 'x-api-key',
so a drill against it without one measures the middleware and nothing else.
A value written as ${NAME} is read from the environment at k6 init and the run refuses to
start when it is unset — so a real key is passed in, never committed here. An entry in
'traffic' may carry its own 'headers' object, which is merged over these for that endpoint.
Empty on purpose. No fiscal traffic mix ships with this repository: FiscalServer is inert
until it is enabled, and which of its routes are worth loading is an operator's choice, not
a default. Adding one is this object plus entries in 'traffic', and nothing else.
Example: "set": { "x-api-key": "${FISCAL_API_KEY}" }
The application UNDER TEST, one entry per connection string, mirroring its Maximum Pool Size
values. Two things read this: the pre-flight, which takes 'app.database' as the drill's
PGDATABASE, and the verdict, which watches each database for connections pinned flat at its
ceiling — that is how 'the pool is the ceiling' is told apart from 'Postgres is the ceiling',
two failures that look identical from the outside and have opposite fixes.
This is NOT the fleet budget. The whole fleet is 'deployment.deployments' below; these are
only the databases that exist on the drill box and can therefore be sampled.
The fleet sharing one Postgres, which is what max_connections is actually sized from. Every
deployment gets its own pool set, because they are not the same size: Waa carries a users
database, FiscalServer is headless and carries none.
The verdict adds them up for the steady total, then adds the LARGEST single one back for the
length of a drain — during those drain_seconds both slots of the deploying application are up
and each holds its own pools. One deployment drains at a time because that is what a deploy
is: deploy.yml loops over the applications and deploy.sh blocks through the drain. The
'everything drains at once' figure is printed too, but it does not decide the verdict.
Keep this in step with the connection strings in the live inventory. It is the same table as
platform/docs/fiscal/OPERATIONS.md 1.1, which is where the arithmetic is explained.

deployments.name: fiscal
deployments.note: Headless — no users database (ADR-0032 D13). 16 here is the connection-string Maximum Pool Size, not FiscalDbContextExtensions.AppPoolSize, which is a DbContext instance pool and caps no connection; they are deliberately set to the same number.

deployment.note: api.educa.ro is not in this list because it is not deployed. At its proposed 32 + 8 + 2 = 42 it takes steady to 224 and the worst case to 306 of 637, and the sum of the per-role CONNECTION LIMITs to 448 of 637 usable. Both fit since max_connections moved 400 -> 640 on 2026-09-03, and the second number is why it moved: option Full's per-role CONNECTION LIMITs did not fit under the old 397. Add its entry here in the same edit that adds it to the live inventory.
